title: Man. Post. Cap. II: Placeus — Manuscript mediate ratio; before Posterior quaestio de poena
pass_a_gloss: I proposed the same reason of mediate imputation in this very Manuscript in these words. For by participation of this corruption we communicate with Adam's sin, and to it, so to speak, we consent habitually. Who does not see that I distinguish Adam's sin, with which we communicate and to which we habitually consent, from the corruption by which we communicate with him and consent? But that can be nothing else than that first actual of Adam. This therefore I wanted imputed to us, and indeed on account of that very habitual consent. So the Learned Man does not set me against myself, but against a figment of his own mind.
pass_b_english: In this very Manuscript I gave the same account of mediate imputation: by sharing this corruption we communicate with Adam's sin, and we consent to it habitually, so to speak. I am plainly distinguishing Adam's sin—the one we share and habitually consent to—from the corruption through which that sharing and consent happen. That sin can only be Adam's first actual. That is what I wanted charged to us, and for that habitual consent. So the Learned Man pits me not against myself but against a fiction of his own making.
source_text: Eandem rationem, imputationis mediatae in hoc ipso Manuscrito proposui his verbis. Hujus enim corruptionis participatione communicamus peccato Adami, eique, ut ita loquar, habitualiter consentimus. Quis non videt me peccatum Adami cui communicamus, cui habitualiter consentimus, distinguere a corruptione qua ei communicamus & consentimus? Id autem aliud esse non potest quam primum illud actuale Adami. Hoc igitur volui nobis imputari, & quidem ob istum ipsum habitualem consensum. Non igitur me mecum committit Vir doctus, sed cum animi sui figmento.
